choices.text: Assign 27A outbound and add a check-in reminder to request or choose a window on the return as soon as the map opens.
Assign 12C outbound for quicker deplaning and leave the return to automatic assignment.
Assign 9B outbound because it is closer to the front and ask for an aisle on the return.
Do not pick any outbound seat now; ask the airport agent to optimize both legs on travel day.

probes.difficulty_rationale: The front-cabin aisle is a normal business-travel choice, and the closed return map prevents a complete assignment. The deciding distinction is how to handle only the seat location within those limits.
probes.gold_action: Assign the available window seat and track the closed return map for the earliest window request.
probes.label_rationale: For a solo flight with selection open on one leg and deferred on the other, the best handling is to take the available window and preserve that location request when the other map opens. The aisle and front-middle alternatives are viable but do not match Jonah's repeated seat-location handling.
probes.query: Jonah is ticketing a solo SFO-to-Greenville-Spartanburg trip for a pump-controls review. The fare and flights are already selected, standard seat selection is included, and he has given no new seat instruction. On the outbound map, 27A is the only no-fee window; 12C and 18D aisles are open, and 9B middle is the closest remaining seat to the front. The return carrier says seats open at online check-in. What should the booking note say?

choices.text: Assign 16C aisle now and add a note to swap to a standard window if one opens before or at check-in.
Take the nearest-front middle seat now so the reservation has a confirmed assignment.
Leave the seat unassigned and enter only a generic best-available note for check-in.
Assign 21D aisle now and add no follow-up note.

probes.difficulty_rationale: Two aisle assignments are similar from the prompt alone, and there is no direct seat to choose. The differentiator is whether the fallback remains tied to a later window opportunity.
probes.gold_action: Use an aisle only because no included window is available, while keeping a window swap on the follow-up list.
probes.label_rationale: When no acceptable window is open, an aisle backup is the right operational fallback, but the window should still be pursued if it appears later. Taking a middle seat just to move forward, or omitting the follow-up, misses the established seat-location pattern.
probes.query: Jonah is completing checkout for a solo Bay Area-to-Bismarck site visit. The chosen itinerary is fixed and the company task is to use included standard seats only. The seat map has no standard windows left: 16C aisle and 21D aisle are open, several middle seats are nearer the front, and the airline allows a note to watch for released seats before check-in. Which seat-handling choice fits best?

choices.text: Assign 25F on the first leg and enter a window request for the regional leg, with a reminder to check the map when it opens.
Assign 14C on the first leg and request an aisle on the regional leg to keep the seat type consistent.
Skip seat selection on both legs because the second map is closed.
Assign 20D now and leave the regional leg without a request so the airline can auto-seat him.

probes.difficulty_rationale: The aisle-consistency option is reasonable if only the current maps are considered. The harder step is separating a closed seat map from an absent seat instruction.
probes.gold_action: Choose the available window and place a window request for the leg where assignment is deferred.
probes.label_rationale: The closed regional map is a limitation to note, not a reason to abandon seat handling. Jonah's solo bookings repeatedly use a window where available and carry the same request forward when selection opens later.
probes.query: Jonah's solo San Jose-to-Duluth trip is ready to issue on the selected flights. The first leg shows a free 25F window and free aisles 14C and 20D; the connecting leg is on a regional aircraft whose seats cannot be chosen until check-in, but the booking form accepts one seat-location request. No companion is traveling. What instruction should go with the ticket?

choices.text: Assign 24A window as the default standard seat.
Assign 11C aisle because it is closer to the front.
Assign 18D aisle to avoid the rear cabin.
Leave the seat unassigned until check-in.

probes.difficulty_rationale: A front aisle is a defensible generic pick, and the trip is personal rather than a plant visit. The distinction depends on carrying the solo seat-location pattern across contexts.
probes.gold_action: Assign a standard window seat for Jonah's solo personal flight.
probes.label_rationale: The repeated solo-flight handling transfers to a personal trip when no companion seating need is present. The closer aisle is plausible, but it should not displace the standard window choice.
probes.query: Jonah is booking a solo personal flight from SFO to Chicago for a weekend memorial. The itinerary is fixed, standard seat selection is included, and he has not added any current seat note. Open standard seats are 11C aisle, 24A window, 25F window, 18D aisle, and 28B middle. Which assignment should the planner make?

choices.text: Choose 22F outbound and 19A return.
Choose 10C outbound and 12D return for easier boarding and deplaning.
Choose one aisle and one window to keep options balanced.
Skip seat assignments and let the airline assign at check-in.

probes.difficulty_rationale: The itinerary details do not favor one seat type on timing, cost, or feasibility. The answer turns on transferring a repeated solo-flight choice to a leisure weekend.
probes.gold_action: Select standard window seats on both solo personal legs.
probes.label_rationale: With seat maps open and no traveling companion, the normal solo handling is to take windows on each leg. The aisle pair is a credible generic alternative, but it is not the better fit for Jonah.
probes.query: Jonah is flying alone to Los Angeles for a Saturday museum opening and returning Sunday evening. The selected carrier includes standard seat selection both ways. The outbound has 22F window and 10C aisle; the return has 19A window and 12D aisle. No one else is on the reservation, and no new seat instruction is written in the trip note. What should be done with seats?

choices.text: Assign 30A on the transborder leg, take 21C where no window is open, and set an alert to move to a window if one appears.
Assign 16C and 21C so both legs are aisles.
Assign 30A and leave the domestic leg unassigned until check-in.
Assign 16C on the transborder leg and 23B on the domestic leg to stay farther forward.

probes.difficulty_rationale: Both A and B avoid middle seats and are operationally clean. The harder distinction is choosing mixed seat handling because availability differs by leg.
probes.gold_action: Use a window where available, use the aisle backup where no window is open, and watch for a later window swap.
probes.label_rationale: The personal context does not change the solo seat handling, and the no-window leg calls for an aisle backup rather than abandoning the window on the other leg. This also respects the limit that a different seat is used only when the window is not available.
probes.query: Jonah has a solo personal ticket to Montreal for a long weekend after a work stop. The flights are already selected in regular economy. On the transborder leg, 30A window and 16C aisle are no-fee; on the domestic positioning leg, only aisle 21C and middle 23B are no-fee, with a seat-change alert available. Which seat note should be entered?

choices.text: Assign the adjacent 29B/29C pair so they sit together, noting that no adjacent window pair is open.
Assign 18A and 24F so both get windows even though they are separated.
Put Jonah in 18A and his spouse in 15C to give Jonah a window and keep her forward.
Leave both unassigned and hope an adjacent pair opens at the airport.

probes.difficulty_rationale: The adjacent pair is less attractive by row and seat type, while the separate windows are clean no-fee options. The deciding point is the companion seating priority rather than generic seat comfort.
probes.gold_action: Seat Jonah and his spouse together, even though that means giving up separate window seats.
probes.label_rationale: When his spouse is on the reservation, Jonah has treated sitting together as more important than preserving a solo window. The separate windows are tempting but should not split them.
probes.query: Jonah and his spouse are ticketing a Friday-Monday trip to Victoria, B.C. on one reservation. The selected fare includes free standard seats. The only adjacent pair left is 29B/29C in the last standard row; separate window seats are open at 18A and 24F, and aisle seats 15C and 16D are also open. No one has asked for a specific side of the plane. Which seat plan should be used?

choices.text: Assign 17C/17D as the side-by-side pair.
Assign 9A and 10A so both travelers get separate windows closer to the front.
Assign Jonah 9A and his spouse 11C to give Jonah a window and keep both near the front.
Skip assignments now and look for a better pair at check-in.

probes.difficulty_rationale: The front windows are individually better seats, and all options are free. The answer depends on recognizing when the solo window rule gives way to a seating-together need.
probes.gold_action: Take the available adjacent pair on the 2-by-2 aircraft.
probes.label_rationale: For spouse travel, Jonah's prior decisions put the pair together ahead of ideal individual seats. A nearby separate window for each traveler is a strong alternative, but it should not split the reservation.
probes.query: Jonah and his spouse are ready to ticket a short weekend flight to Calgary on a 2-by-2 aircraft. Standard seats are free. A side-by-side pair 17C/17D is open; separate window seats 9A and 10A are open closer to the front, and 11C/12C aisles are open. The fare, flight times, and cabin are already decided. What should the seat instruction be?

choices.text: Assign 24A window.
Assign 13C aisle so he sits next to the colleague.
Assign 18B middle to stay closer to the colleague's row without changing his reservation.
Leave Jonah unassigned until check-in in case the colleague moves.

probes.difficulty_rationale: Sitting by a colleague is a reasonable generic coordination choice, especially on the same flight. The key distinction is that the prompt removes any onboard coordination need.
probes.gold_action: Assign Jonah a standard window seat because there is no actual onboard seating need with the colleague.
probes.label_rationale: A colleague on the same flight is not enough by itself to override Jonah's solo seat handling. The companion-together exceptions apply when sitting together is the trip need; here they are simply meeting after arrival.
probes.query: Jonah is on the same Monday flight to Milwaukee as a distributor colleague, but they are on separate reservations and plan to meet at the rental-car counter; no onboard prep is planned. Jonah's fare includes standard seat selection. Open standard seats include 24A window, 25F window, 13C aisle next to the colleague's 13B, and 18B middle. Which seat should be assigned for Jonah?

choices.text: Delta SFO-MSP-MLI: depart 1:05 p.m., 1h35m in MSP, arrive 8:50 p.m., $516.
United SFO-DEN-ORD-MLI: depart 12:40 p.m., connect 1h10m in DEN and 1h05m in ORD, arrive 8:25 p.m., $478.
American SFO-DFW-MLI: depart 11:50 a.m., 4h55m in DFW, arrive 10:10 p.m., $462.
Alaska/American SFO-SEA-ORD-MLI: depart 12:15 p.m., connect 1h20m in SEA and 1h15m in ORD, arrive 9:05 p.m., $489.

probes.difficulty_rationale: The nearest alternative is cheaper, United, and arrives slightly earlier, so the prompt alone makes it attractive. The deciding distinction is connection count and connection quality.
probes.gold_action: Lead with the one-stop itinerary that has a reasonable transfer and no extended airport sit.
probes.label_rationale: The selected line is the only one with a single reasonable connection and no long airport sit. Cheaper or United options ask Jonah to accept either two hops or an extended layover without a current reason.
probes.query: Jonah is sketching Bay Area-to-Quad Cities travel for a Monday arrival before a Tuesday equipment checkout in Davenport. There is no Monday client dinner, the hotel will hold a late arrival, and all fares below are regular economy within approval range. Which flight plan should lead the note?

choices.text: Delta SFO-MSP-TVC: depart 12:55 p.m., 1h20m in MSP, arrive 7:35 p.m., $438.
American SFO-ORD-TVC: depart 1:15 p.m., 45m in ORD, arrive 6:55 p.m., $415.
United SFO-DEN-ORD-TVC: depart 12:30 p.m., connect 1h05m in DEN and 1h10m in ORD, arrive 7:10 p.m., $421.
Delta SFO-DTW-TVC: depart 11:35 a.m., 4h10m in DTW, arrive 9:25 p.m., $402.

probes.difficulty_rationale: The near miss is less expensive and arrives earlier, while every option is feasible. The choice turns on the quality of the single connection, not on basic schedule viability.
probes.gold_action: Hold the one-stop option with a comfortable connection rather than the tighter, two-stop, or long-sit alternatives.
probes.label_rationale: The personal weekend still involves a small-market connecting itinerary, and Jonah's repeated handling favors one reasonable layover. The cheaper earlier arrival through ORD is close, but the transfer is the fragile part.
probes.query: Jonah is planning a solo Friday flight from the Bay Area to Traverse City for a volunteer trail weekend. He can leave after a late-morning call, the lodge accepts arrivals until 10 p.m., and all options get him there Friday without checked bags. Which outbound should be held first?

choices.text: American SFO-DFW-CLL: depart 12:20 p.m., 1h30m in DFW, arrive 5:45 p.m., $525.
United SFO-IAH-CLL: depart 12:50 p.m., 48m in Houston, arrive 5:20 p.m., $508.
United SFO-DEN-IAH-CLL: depart 11:55 a.m., connect 1h15m in DEN and 1h05m in Houston, arrive 5:35 p.m., $486.
American SFO-DFW-CLL: depart 10:45 a.m., 3h55m in DFW, arrive 6:40 p.m., $489.

probes.difficulty_rationale: The closest distractor wins on carrier, price, and arrival time, so the prompt alone does not settle the tradeoff. The decisive factor is avoiding a tight transfer while keeping the trip to one stop.
probes.gold_action: Recommend the single-connection routing with the more comfortable DFW transfer.
probes.label_rationale: The United one-stop is cheaper and earlier, but a sub-hour transfer is exactly the type of fragile connection Jonah has pushed back on. The two-hop and long-sit options are viable but worse fits absent a stronger current constraint.
probes.query: Jonah needs a Monday arrival in College Station for a Tuesday analyzer kickoff. The site has no Monday event; reaching the hotel by early evening is enough. The listed regular-economy fares are all approvable, and the rental-car plan is the same either way. Which routing should be recommended first?
